records.sourceFile: A cherry tree ripe for picking - The relationship between the acute-chronic workload ratio and health problems.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Resolved 2026-10-13 (Codex review finding). Crossref and doi.org check for 10.2519/jospt.2021.9893.

records.evidenceSummary: A prospective cohort of 86 elite U-19 football players (47 male, 39 female, from six teams) logged daily training load (session RPE times duration) and health problems for 105 days, recording 196 health problems. Of 108 random-effects analyses of acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) variants against three health outcomes, the text reports 24 (22%) as significant, while Table 2 and the figure add up to 22; significance was most common with EWMA-based ACWR and low-versus-high comparisons. The authors frame the study as a critique showing that results depend on method choices.
records.limitations: Daily self-report questionnaires that were not validated, with 31% of daily questionnaires unanswered and no adjustment for sex, age or clustering in the main models. Only about one in five analyses was significant and the authors state the study is not evidence for an ACWR-injury relationship, so the paper cannot show that ACWR predicts health problems.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff may read the significant ACWR associations as evidence that ACWR predicts injury, when the authors present the study as a critique of methods and say it is not evidence for that relationship.

findings: largest OR attributed to 'non-coupled 7:28 rolling-average z-score' from the figure label -> assigned to coupled 7:21 EWMA pre-defined, where Table 2 low-to-high ranges put the 15.25 upper CI (EWMA, 21-day, coupled, pre-defined) and text says 'coupled 7-day acute, 21-day chronic ... EWMA ... pre-defined categories (OR: 5.27)' and figure row labels contradict Table 2 (figure shows non-coupled rows with 15 significant results, Table 2 gives non-coupled 7 (19%))

records.sourceFile: A Review of the Validity and Reliability of Accelerometer-Based Metrics From Upper Back–Mounted GNSS Player Tracking Systems for Athlete Training Load Monitoring.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Crossref title match (similarity 1.0) on 2026-10-12; doi.org HTTP 200

records.evidenceSummary: A narrative review of accelerometer-based load metrics (PlayerLoad, Body Load, Dynamic Stress Load) from upper back-mounted GNSS units in team sports. The authors report that reliability of the raw accelerometer data is mostly high to very high, while metric reliability and validity against motion capture and ground reaction force vary with filtering, device and activity. Links to internal load and injury are mixed: the main injury result cited is a 4-week PlayerLoad accumulation with an AUC of 0.585, which the authors call moderate.
records.limitations: The review describes no search strategy or inclusion criteria, so the evidence base cannot be checked for completeness. Most validity and reliability data come from single devices, specific filters and short activity protocols, and the authors note that internal biomechanical load is rarely measured.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff may treat PlayerLoad or Dynamic Stress Load as valid measures of tissue load or injury risk, when the review finds the injury and internal-load links are weak or mixed and the metrics are not comparable across devices, manufacturers or athletes.

changes: evidenceSummary/findings/rtp: 'moderate association' for injury stated without context -> AUC 0.585 (95% CI 0.482-0.672) reported as the authors' 'moderate' label, with note that the printed CI includes 0.5

findings: 'metrics correlate moderately to very highly with distance' generalized PlayerLoad to all metrics -> PlayerLoad r = 0.70 to 0.98; Dynamic Stress Load 'no correlation (r = -0.01) with distance covered per minute' in futsal
findings: 'mostly good CVs' applied to raw data only -> added that metric CVs were poor in Barreira et al. (PL CV 14.5-24.5%, Table 5)

practicalImplications: recommendation to use PlayerLoadSlow for rugby collisions removed -> Hulin et al. 'reported a lower correlation for PlayerLoadSlow ... should be used with caution'; added authors' 20 Hz / 10 Hz filtering guidance

records.sourceFile: A systematic review and meta-analysis of wearable satellite system technology for liner sprint profiling - Technological innovations and practical applications.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Crossref title match (similarity 0.997) on 2026-10-12; doi.org HTTP 200

records.evidenceSummary: A systematic review with meta-analysis of 16 concurrent validity and reliability studies of GNSS sensors for linear sprint profiling in athletes from recreationally trained to elite level (PubMed and SPORTDiscus, searched to July 2023). Against radar or laser criteria, pooled standardized mean differences were small for maximal sprint speed (d = 0.22, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.42, the only estimate whose CI excluded zero), tau, V0, relative F0 and relative Pmax, with moderate to high heterogeneity. Sampling rate and manufacturer moderated results, and the acceleration metrics tau and F0 showed weaker agreement and reliability than speed metrics.
records.limitations: Only 16 small studies were retained, the meta-analysis used radar- or laser-criterion data only, and heterogeneity was high across devices, filters, protocols and criteria. Several manufacturers' processing steps are undisclosed, so the pooled estimates cannot be applied to a specific device without checking its own validity.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff may read the small pooled effects as proof that any GNSS device gives valid sprint-profile metrics, when tau and F0 had poor signal-to-noise and CVs above 5%, and agreement depended on sampling rate, filtering and manufacturer.

changes: findings: 'most with radar or laser criteria' was wrong -> radar (3,11,13,36,45) and laser (32,45,56) cover 7 studies; timing gates (2,3,5,31,48), video (6) and sliding platform (1) the rest
findings/evidenceSummary: added that MSS is the only pooled CI excluding zero and that at >=10 Hz MSS SMD was 0.11 (95% CI -0.04 to 0.26) (Table 5)

synthesisCaution/practicalImplications: Pmax grouped with tau and F0 as weakly reliable -> text reports 'CVs <5% for MSS, V0, and relative Pmax, whereas F0 and t were >5%' and signal-to-noise 'good for MSS, V0, and Pmax, but poor for F0 and t'

limitations: timing-gate statement sharpened to 'timing gates ... overestimates certain FV metrics associated with the acceleration phase'; added 'only 2 GNSS studies reported all specific filtering specifications'
populations: added Healthy Athletes (exclusion criterion: 'subjects had any musculoskeletal disorders')

records.sourceFile: Focused review of sleep wearable technology and its application in sports performance.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Crossref title match (similarity 1.0) on 2026-10-12; doi.org HTTP 200

records.evidenceSummary: Narrative review of actigraphy and consumer sleep wearable studies in athletes and non-athletes, which the authors state is more narrative than structured. Wearables detect sleep reasonably well but are weaker at detecting wake, with wake accuracy of about 49% to 60% in validation studies. The authors report that proprietary summary sleep scores have no identified link to training, performance or recovery.
records.limitations: The review describes no search or selection method and presents no new data. The authors note that the field has few studies, many of them industry sponsored, so the review cannot show whether wearable sleep data change performance or recovery outcomes.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read a consumer sleep score as a validated measure of recovery, when the authors state its clinical meaning is unknown.

changes: screeningLimitations: 'Most validation work is industry sponsored, and few studies are athlete-specific' overstated the text -> now 'few studies, many of them industry sponsored' ('there are currently few research studies, and many of these are done with industry sponsorship')
verification.residualConcerns: The rtp field touches concussion detection; the paper only says wearables 'represent an opportunity' and are 'likely not sensitive or specific', so it must not be cited as support for wearable-based concussion screening.

records.sourceFile: Height restrictions for dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry - What are our options for body composition and bone health precision.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Crossref title match (similarity 1.0) on 2026-10-12; doi.org HTTP 200

records.evidenceSummary: Cross-sectional DXA precision study of 60 adults (34.8 +/- 11.9 years; 30 men and 30 women; mean BMI 26) who had three total-body scans on a GE Lunar Prodigy (n = 15) or Hologic Horizon A (n = 45), with one GE Lunar iDXA used for exploratory analysis. A combined scan built from an upper-body region of the head-first scan and a lower-body region of the flipped scan added 0.25% to 0.63% error on the Lunar Prodigy, but added about 4.35% BMC error on the Horizon A and 3.71% BMC error on the iDXA.

records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the combined-scan method as a precise way to track any tall athlete on any DXA model, when the bone mineral content error was large on the newer Hologic and GE units.

records.sourceFile: PEP - A tackle value measuring the prevention of expected points.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Resolved 2026-10-13 (Codex review finding). Crossref and doi.org check for 10.48550/arxiv.2407.08508.

records.evidenceSummary: Methodological study that develops a tackle-value metric, prevented expected points (PEP), from NFL 2022 tracking data for 11,313 tackles across the first nine weeks of the season. The metric compares the observed end-of-play yard line with a random-forest prediction for the hypothetical play in which the tackle was missed, converts the difference to expected points, and fits a mixed-effects model to estimate each tackler's effect. The authors report that the top-ranked tacklers are sensible when compared with leaderboard data, but they do not validate PEP against outcomes.
records.limitations: The metric is built from one half-season of tracking data and has no external validation against outcomes. The authors state that passing plays may favor cornerbacks who allow catches, and that missed tackles are excluded from the main analysis.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could treat the PEP tackler ranking as a definitive measure of tackling ability, when the authors describe it as one piece of a wider evaluation, with known biases on pass plays and a single season of data.

changes: paper.findings: 'top three 2022 leaderboard inside linebackers' -> top three players on the 2022 NFL tackles leaderboard ('the top three players from the 2022 NFL tackles leaderboard (Nick Bolton, Foyesade Oluokun, and Jordyn Brooks) are all found in top ten inside linebackers')
verification.residualConcerns: Resolved 2026-10-13: DOI changed to the arXiv v1 DOI (10.48550/arXiv.2407.08508) to match the arXiv v1 PDF that was read. The journal-version DOI is no longer used.

records.sourceFile: Percentile rankings and position differences for absolute and allometrically scaled performance measures from the NFL Scouting Combine.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Crossref title match (similarity 0.927) on 2026-10-12; doi.org HTTP 200

records.evidenceSummary: Cross-sectional normative analysis of 3,015 players at the NFL Scouting Combine from 2015 to 2019, giving percentile ranks and means for the 40-yd dash (with 10- and 20-yd splits), bench press repetitions, vertical and broad jump, pro agility and L-cone times, both raw and allometrically scaled to body mass. Absolute results showed skill positions (DB, WR) fastest and highest jumping, with linemen strongest on the bench press, and after allometric scaling DL, LB, RB and TE tended to score highest while QB and OL scored lowest.

records.sourceFile: Position-Specific Differences in Speed Profiles Among National Football League Scouting Combine Participants.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Crossref title match (similarity 1.0) on 2026-10-12; doi.org HTTP 200

records.evidenceSummary: This cross-sectional analysis used publicly available NFL Scouting Combine data from 2,156 American football players (2017, 2018, 2019, 2022 and 2023) with valid 40-yard dash and 10- and 20-yard split times. The authors calculated maximal velocity (vmax), acceleration time constant (t) and maximal acceleration (amax) from the splits, compared eight position groups with one-way ANOVA, and correlated these variables with other combine tests. Skill positions (DB and WR) had the highest vmax and amax and the lowest t, and offensive linemen had the lowest vmax and amax and the highest t.
records.limitations: The speed profiles are estimated from split times in a single testing setting, and the study has no training, injury or on-field data. The position differences are cross-sectional and cannot show what causes them, and the authors note that body size and position selection may explain part of the gap.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the position gaps as the result of position-specific training, when the author could not separate training adaptation from body size and selection for each position.

records.sourceFile: Practitioner usage, applications, and understanding of wearable GPS and accelerometer technology in team sports.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Crossref title match (similarity 1.0) on 2026-10-12; doi.org HTTP 200

records.evidenceSummary: This cross-sectional online survey (May 2021 to May 2022) asked 72 practitioners who regularly use GPS and accelerometer load monitoring in outdoor or invasion team sports about their usage, understanding and opinions. All respondents supported GPS use, 87.5% agreed that wearable data informs training prescription, and only 50% agreed that it influences decisions in competition. GPS metrics were used and understood more than accelerometer-derived metrics, with 47.2% agreeing that accelerometer metrics are easy to understand, and 93.1% said wearable technology needs further standardization.
records.limitations: This is a self-selected survey of practitioners' opinions and reported practice, not a measure of athlete load, validity or outcomes. Respondents were not asked to separate sports or competition levels, and self-rated understanding did not match the quality of the definitions they gave.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read these practitioner opinions as evidence about how accurate or useful the wearable metrics are, when the survey measured what practitioners believe and do, not whether the metrics are valid.

records.sourceFile: Predicting sprint performance from the vertical and horizontal jumps in National Football League Combine athletes.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Crossref title match (similarity 1.0) on 2026-10-12; doi.org HTTP 200

records.evidenceSummary: This retrospective analysis used publicly available NFL Combine data from 1999 to 2020 and split the players into a training set (n = 2,071) and a test set (n = 2,070). Regression equations predicted 9.14-m, 9.14 to 18.29-m, 18.29 to 36.58-m and 36.58-m sprint times from vertical jump, broad jump, height and body mass, with adjusted R2 values of 0.74 to 0.84. In the test set, biases were -0.05 to -0.02 s and RMSE was 0.05 to 0.12 s, with 5 to 6% of predictions outside the limits of agreement.
records.limitations: The equations come from one retrospective data set of NFL Combine testing, using a hand-trigger, three-point sprint start and a Vertec vertical jump, and they were fitted with stepwise regression on a single random split. Their accuracy in other squads, other sprint setups or other jump methods is untested, and the paper's own sample counts disagree (see limitations).
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could treat the predicted sprint time as the athlete's true sprint ability, or read a faster or slower actual time as a technical or physical deficit, when 5 to 6% of predictions fell outside the agreement limits and the authors say the gap needs further investigation.

changes: paper.findings: 'standard errors of 0.05 to 0.12 s' -> 0.04 to 0.12 s ('9.14- to 18.29-m time (adjusted R2 = 0.74, SEE = 0.04 seconds)')

paper.tldr: use of predicted-vs-actual gap framed as the authors' proposal, not a validated finding ('coaches should view the difference ... as an item that warrants further investigation')

records.sourceFile: Selecting Metrics That Matter - Comparing the Use of the Countermovement Jump for Performance Profiling, Neuromuscular Fatigue Monitoring, and I.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Crossref title match (similarity 0.909) on 2026-10-12; doi.org HTTP 200

records.evidenceSummary: Narrative review, with no search method described, of how countermovement jump (CMJ) metrics should be chosen for performance profiling, neuromuscular fatigue monitoring and injury rehabilitation testing. Jump height and peak power track strength and speed, but a meta-analysis cited by the authors found maximal jump height and peak power were not sensitive to fatigue (ES -0.04 each), while other cited studies found time-based metrics such as flight time and time to peak power changed more after intense exercise and over 24-72 h. Tables 2 and 3 use example data (20 athletes, stated to be hypothetical; 3 athletes) to show how a change is judged against the test's coefficient of variation.
records.limitations: The paper gives no search strategy, so the selection of evidence cannot be reproduced and its completeness cannot be judged. Several recommendations rest on the authors' own experience and on correlations, and the worked examples are not real athlete data.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could take the metric choices as validated for their own squads, or read the worked examples as real athlete results.

evidenceSummary, paper.methods, paper.limitations, synthesisCaution: Table 3 called hypothetical -> only Table 2 is stated to be hypothetical ('This data is hypothetical'); Table 3 is 'example data for 3 individual athletes'

records.sourceFile: Subjective wellness acute-chronic workloads and injury risk in college football.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Crossref title match (similarity 1.0) on 2026-10-12; doi.org HTTP 200

records.evidenceSummary: Retrospective analysis of one 17-week NCAA Division I football season: 42 players, 1,807 aligned daily workload and wellness records, and 55 noncontact injuries. Injury risk over the next 3 days was very likely higher when the 7:21-day EWMA acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) was 2 SD above (RR 3.05, 90% CI 1.14 to 8.16) or 2 SD below (RR 2.49, 90% CI 1.11 to 5.58) the mean, and wellness showed no clear association with injury.
records.limitations: This is a single-team, single-season observational analysis, and the authors say the interaction tests were likely underpowered. Only field-based workloads were measured, so the findings cannot separate ACWR effects from unmeasured resistance work, academic stress or positional demands.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the high-ACWR with 'better' soreness result as a reliable warning sign, when it is an exploratory interaction with wide intervals in one team, and it does not supply a validated load threshold.

changes: limitations: 'the abstract overstates them' -> both abstract and results label the overall-wellness interactions 'likely' under magnitude-based inference although 90% CIs include 1 ('likely higher risk ... (RR: 1.52, 90% CI: 0.91-2.54)'); added the abstract misprint '0.83 to 674' versus results '0.83-6.74'

records.sourceFile: Terminology and Interpretation Across Neuromuscular Profiling Methods - A Systematic Review.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Crossref title match (similarity 1.0) on 2026-10-12; doi.org HTTP 200

records.evidenceSummary: Systematic review (PRISMA guidelines, protocol not pre-registered) of PubMed, Scopus and SPORTDiscus searches to September 2024: 10,574 records identified, 1,653 assessed for eligibility and 184 included, covering 209 neuromuscular profiling outputs from six methods (DSI, EUR, RSI, RSImod, force-velocity profiling and impulse analysis). records.sourceFile: The deceleration deficit - A novel field-based method to quantify deceleration during change of direction performance.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Crossref title match (similarity 1.0) on 2026-10-12; doi.org HTTP 200

records.evidenceSummary: Cross-sectional study of 36 university-level invasion-sport athletes (19 women, 17 men; mean age 20.3 years) who completed 505 change-of-direction trials in both turning directions and 15-m sprints in one session. records.synthesisCaution: Staff could treat DD as a validated measure of deceleration ability that pinpoints each athlete's limiter, when the paper shows only correlations from one session and calls for reliability and validity work.

records.sourceFile: The Reliability, Bias, Differences, and Agreement Between Velocity Measurement Devices During the Hang Clean Pull.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Crossref title match (similarity 1.0) on 2026-10-12; doi.org HTTP 200

records.evidenceSummary: Repeated-measures, cross-sectional validation study in 14 resistance-trained men (mean age 25.5 years, at least 4 years of training experience) who performed hang clean pulls at seven loads from 20% to 140% of their 1RM hang power clean. A GymAware PowerTool and a Tendo Power Analyzer were attached to the barbell and compared for reliability, bias and agreement. Both devices were reliable for mean barbell velocity (ICC 0.93 to 0.97), and the Tendo overestimated mean and peak barbell velocity by 3.7 to 6.8% and 1.8 to 2.9%, with small between-device effect sizes (MBV g = 0.35 to 0.57; PBV g = 0.23 to 0.54).
records.limitations: The GymAware was used as the criterion device because 3D motion capture was unavailable, and the sample was resistance-trained men only, so results may not transfer to other populations or to women. The authors note that few comparable studies exist for this lift, and that the Tendo's peak velocity reliability fell at heavier loads.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the device agreement as proof that the two velocity devices can be swapped freely, when the authors say they calculate velocity differently and should not be used interchangeably, especially at 140% 1RM.

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Crossref title match (similarity 1.0) on 2026-10-12; doi.org HTTP 200

records.evidenceSummary: Retrospective analysis of 15 years of data from 496 first-year NCAA Division 1 football players from one program (big positions n = 122, mid n = 178, skill n = 196), who completed the 40-yard sprint, pro-agility and L drill tests, with momentum calculated from body mass and average velocity. Positional differences were moderate to very large, and starters were faster and had greater momentum than nonstarters with small to moderate effects (for example, 40-yard sprint of 5.18 vs 5.30 s in big positions). ROC cutoffs to separate starters from nonstarters had AUC values of 0.57 to 0.76 (poor to fair) and positive predictive values of 15% to 43%.
records.limitations: All data came from one program under a single head coach, and starter status was the only selection outcome, so the results may reflect that program's style of play and selection decisions. The ROC thresholds discriminated poorly, and the study tested athletes after a 6-week winter program, not at other times of the year.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could use the ROC cutoffs as a way to pick or cut players, when the authors found the thresholds had poor to fair discrimination and low positive predictive value, and they advise against using them for selection.

changes: limitations: added hand timing, first-year testing vs career starter status, and the Table 5 AUC label inconsistency (0.57 labelled 'fair')
athleteDev: position priorities stated as directives -> attributed to the authors as recommendations from cross-sectional data

records.sourceFile: Training Impulse and Session Ratings of Perceived Exertion as Perceived by Athletes and Observed by Coaches During Preseason Football Camp.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Crossref title match (similarity 1.0) on 2026-10-12; doi.org HTTP 200

records.evidenceSummary: Prospective study of 24 NCAA Division II football athletes (6 first-year, 18 returning) and 2 coaches over the first 6 days of preseason camp. It compares heart-rate training impulse (Edwards TRIMP, from chest-strap monitors) with session RPE load rated by athletes and by one football coach and one strength and conditioning coach. The authors report significant but low-to-moderate correlations (athletes r = 0.62, football coach r = 0.68, strength and conditioning coach r = 0.49), stronger in first-year athletes, and conclude the measures are not interchangeable.
records.limitations: Agreement was assessed with correlations only, not bias or limits of agreement, and the 139 observations are repeated measures on 24 athletes from one team. Each coach role is a single person, so coach findings describe two individuals, not coach types. Maximal heart rate was mostly estimated (220 minus age), and the paper has several internal numerical inconsistencies.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read these correlations as showing that coach observation or athlete ratings can replace heart-rate monitoring, or that football coaches judge load better than strength coaches in general. The authors say the measures are not interchangeable, and the coach comparison rests on one coach of each type.

records.sourceFile: Velocity-Based Training With Weightlifting Derivatives - Barbell and System Velocity Comparisons.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: Crossref title match (similarity 1.0) on 2026-10-12; doi.org HTTP 200

records.evidenceSummary: Repeated-measures study in 14 resistance-trained men who were not competitive weightlifters. Each performed three individual repetitions per load of the jump shrug, hang high pull, hang power clean, hang clean pull and countermovement shrug across 4 to 7 loads (20% to 140% of hang power clean 1RM), measured with a barbell linear position transducer and a force platform. Mean and peak barbell velocities were significantly greater than system (body plus bar) velocities at every exercise and load (p < 0.001, Hedges g at least 1.49), and the authors conclude the two measures should not be substituted for one another.
records.limitations: Only individual repetitions were tested, not sets, and several loads (20% to 40% of hang power clean 1RM) are lighter than these lifts are usually prescribed; system velocity was not maximal at the lightest loads for four exercises. The sample was 14 men who were not competitive weightlifters, so generalization to women, weightlifters or other groups is limited.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could treat a device's barbell velocity as a measure of whole-body velocity, or apply mean-velocity zones built for squats to these pulls. The study shows the two velocities differ greatly; the authors' advice to use peak velocity and to pick exercises for force or velocity emphasis is their interpretation, not something the study tested.
